01.r: Joins this arrival to what goes before.

02.r: Jesus and his disciples arrive in the city.
02.n: A present tense in a past narrative, as Mark often writes, which makes the scene vivid. The KJV, ASV and YLT keep it; the others turn it into a past tense.

04.n: Abbott-Smith records two Greek forms of the name: this one, Hierosolyma, a neuter plural, and the indeclinable Ierousalem. He notes that Mark always uses the former.

05.r: Moves to what Jesus does in the city.

06.r: Jesus goes into the temple grounds before he acts.
06.n: An aorist participle: the entering comes first, then the driving out.

09.r: Marks his entry into the temple.

11.r: The whole temple area, courts included, where the trading went on.
11.n: This study renders ἱερόν 'temple' and keeps 'sanctuary' for ναός, the shrine itself. ἱερόν takes in the whole sacred precinct with its courts, which is why the BSB says 'temple courts'.

12.r: Jesus starts to clear the traders out.
12.n: Abbott-Smith gives the active senses 'to begin' and 'to rule'; the middle, as here, means to begin, and his entry connects its use with an infinitive to Aramaic usage. Mark has this 'began to' where Matthew's account of the same event has only 'drove out'.

13.r: He forces the traders out of the temple area.
13.n: Abbott-Smith: 'to drive, cast or send out, to expel'. A present infinitive after 'began': the driving out was under way.

14.r: The article turns 'selling' into a description of people.

15.r: The traders who sold goods in the temple area.
15.n: Abbott-Smith gives the first sense as 'to exchange or barter', the second 'to sell', and lists this verse under the second.

17.r: A second article: buyers are named as a group of their own.
17.n: Of the six translations only the ASV shows this second article, with 'and them that bought'.

18.r: The people buying from the traders.
18.n: Abbott-Smith derives the verb from ἀγορά, the market place, and gives the sense 'to buy in the market, purchase'. He lists this verse as a use without an object.

19.r: The trading was going on inside the temple area.

21.r: The temple precinct, named again to stress where the trade was.

24.r: The tables at which the changers did business.
24.n: Abbott-Smith gives first 'a table, dining-table'. The same word came to mean a money changer's table, and later a bank.

25.r: The article; 'of' comes from the genitive case of the noun that follows.

26.r: Men who exchanged one currency for another, for a fee.
26.n: Abbott-Smith derives the word from κόλλυβος, which he glosses 'a small coin, a rate of exchange'. The name therefore points to the fee or small coin charged for the exchange.

27.r: Adds the seats to the tables.

28.r: The particular seats of the dove sellers.

29.r: The seats the dove sellers sat on at their trade.
29.n: Abbott-Smith derives the word from κατά and ἕδρα, a seat, and gives 'a chair, seat'. English 'cathedral', the church that holds a bishop's chair, comes from it.

30.r: The article turns 'selling' into a description of people.

32.r: The doves that were on sale there.

33.r: Birds sold in the temple area, most likely for sacrifice.
33.n: That they were sold for sacrifice is a reasonable inference from where they were sold; the verse does not say so.

34.r: He tips the tables and seats over.
34.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to turn down, turn over', as of soil, and 'to overturn, overthrow', the sense here. The Greek holds the verb back to the end of the sentence, after both tables and seats, as the YLT keeps: 'he overthrew'.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus names the subject, ὁ Ἰησοῦς, 'Jesus', where our text leaves it in the verb. That is why the KJV, Geneva and YLT read 'Jesus went' or 'Jesus having gone', while the DRC and ASV have 'he'.
